body:
Not every trademark identifies a single manufacturer

Ordinary trademarks generally distinguish the goods or services of one commercial source from those of others. However, the Trade Marks Act, 1999 also recognises collective marks and certification marks.

These categories have different purposes. A collective mark identifies a commercial connection with members of an association, whereas a certification mark indicates that specified characteristics have been certified by the mark's proprietor.

Collective trademarks

A collective mark distinguishes the goods or services of members of an association that owns the mark from those of persons outside the association.

Chapter VIII of the Trade Marks Act contains special provisions for collective marks.

Such marks are associated with regulations governing their use. The regulations identify who may use the mark and specify relevant membership and usage conditions.

For example, suppose an association of independent craft producers adopts and registers a collective mark. Its authorised members may use that mark according to the association's regulations.

The mark identifies the goods or services as associated with members of that organisation. It does not necessarily certify that each product has independently passed a government quality examination.

Certification trademarks

A certification mark distinguishes goods or services certified by the proprietor in relation to characteristics such as origin, material, method of manufacture, service performance, quality or accuracy.

Chapter IX of the Trade Marks Act deals with certification trademarks.

Section 70 contains an important restriction: a person carrying on trade in goods of the kind certified, or in services of the kind certified, cannot register the mark as the proprietor of that certification trademark.

This separation helps maintain the distinction between an organisation certifying characteristics and a trader selling the goods or services being certified.

Collective and certification marks compared

FeatureCollective markCertification mark
Principal purposeIdentifies association membershipIdentifies certified characteristics
Typical proprietorAssociation of personsEligible certifying proprietor
Who uses it?Authorised association membersEligible users meeting certification conditions
Relevant chapterChapter VIIIChapter IX

Quality marks and consumer awareness

Consumers frequently encounter product-quality symbols such as the ISI Standard Mark and AGMARK.

The ISI Standard Mark is associated with applicable certification schemes of the Bureau of Indian Standards. AGMARK is associated with grading and certification arrangements for agricultural products.

Their use is governed by the applicable standards and certification laws or schemes. They should not be confused with an ordinary manufacturer's brand name.

The presence of a valid certification or quality mark indicates conformity with the relevant certification requirements. It does not establish that the product is superior in every possible respect.

How trademarks protect consumers

Trademarks help consumers identify the commercial source of goods and services. This supports informed purchasing decisions and allows consumers to associate their experiences with a particular business.

Misleading imitation of packaging or branding can cause consumers to purchase goods under a mistaken belief about commercial origin. Trademark infringement and passing-off remedies can therefore complement broader consumer-protection measures.

The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 separately addresses consumer rights, misleading advertisements and unfair trade practices. These provisions operate alongside intellectual-property laws but have distinct legal purposes.

For example, a falsely advertised product may raise a consumer-protection issue even when there is no copying of another person's registered trademark.

Collective mark: identifies members of an association. Certification mark: identifies goods or services certified as satisfying specified characteristics. Ordinary trademark: identifies commercial origin.

Application to Gujarat's craft sector

Gujarat has established craft traditions involving textiles, embroidery and decorative products. Producers working within associations may find collective identification commercially useful.

For instance, an eligible association of artisans could use a properly registered collective mark to identify products made by its authorised members. A separate certification arrangement could indicate that products satisfy specified quality or manufacturing criteria.

These are different legal mechanisms. The existence of a traditional craft does not itself establish that a particular collective or certification trademark has been registered.

Prelims focus

  • Chapter VIII of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 concerns collective marks.
  • Chapter IX concerns certification marks.
  • Section 61 addresses the application of trademark provisions to collective marks.
  • Section 63 requires regulations governing the use of collective marks.
  • Section 70 restricts registration of certification marks by traders dealing in the goods or services they certify.
  • Trap: Association membership and independent certification of product characteristics are not the same thing.

[Sources: Trade Marks Act, 1999, Sections 2, 61–63 and 69–74, Intellectual Property India; Consumer Protection Act, 2019, Section 2, definitions of misleading advertisement and unfair trade practice; NCERT, Understanding Economic Development, Class 10, Chapter 5, Consumer Rights; NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class 11, Chapter 1, Crafts Heritage; consulted 14 November 2026.]

title: Collective Marks, Certification Marks and Consumer Protection

body:
Meaning of an industrial design

An industrial design concerns specified visual features of an article. These features may make a product recognisable, visually attractive or commercially appealing.

Section 2(d) of the Designs Act, 2000 defines a design through features such as shape, configuration, pattern, ornament and composition of lines or colours applied to an article by an industrial process or means.

The relevant features must appeal to and be judged solely by the eye in the finished article.

Industrial-design law protects qualifying appearance rather than the technical operating principle of the product.

What types of visual features can be protected?

A design may consist of features applied in 2 dimensions, 3 dimensions or both.

  • Shape: the external form of an article, such as the ornamental contour of a container.
  • Configuration: the visual arrangement of elements forming the article.
  • Pattern: repeated decorative features applied to a product surface.
  • Ornament: visual decorative elements contributing to the article's appearance.
  • Composition of lines or colours: qualifying arrangements applied to an article.

For example, a manufacturer may develop a new ornamental pattern for a ceramic container. The pattern may qualify as a design if the relevant statutory requirements are satisfied.

Industrial design and technical function

The Designs Act expressly excludes a mode or principle of construction and anything that is, in substance, merely a mechanical device.

Suppose an engineer invents an improved locking mechanism for a container. The mechanism's technical operating principle is not protected as an industrial design merely because the finished container has a particular appearance.

However, the container may also possess independently eligible visual features. The design inquiry concerns those features rather than the technical principle itself.

Industrial-design protection: statutory protection for qualifying new or original visual features applied to an article, rather than protection for the article's underlying technical working principle.

Conditions for design registration

Section 4 prohibits registration of certain designs. Important grounds include:

  • The design is not new or original.
  • The design was disclosed to the public in India or another country before the relevant filing or priority date, subject to applicable statutory provisions.
  • The design is not significantly distinguishable from known designs or combinations of known designs.
  • The design comprises scandalous or obscene matter.

The definition of a design also excludes specified subject matter, including mere mechanical devices, modes or principles of construction, and the statutory categories of trademarks and artistic works identified in Section 2(d).

Novelty and prior publication

The requirement of newness means that a design cannot ordinarily receive registration if the same design has already been made publicly available in a disqualifying manner.

For example, a manufacturer intending to register a new decorative bottle shape should consider design protection before publicly launching that shape. Prior public disclosure may create a legal obstacle to registration.

The Act contains specific provisions dealing with certain exhibition-related disclosures. For an exhibition notified by the Central Government, Section 21 requires prior notice to the Controller and a registration application within 6 months of first exhibition or publication of the design's description. Therefore, the result depends on the precise statutory conditions rather than a blanket statement that every disclosure produces the same outcome.

How designs are registered

Registration is handled under the Designs Act through the Controller-General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks, acting as Controller of Designs, and authorised officers.

  1. Identify the design: determine the visual features and article for which protection is sought.
  2. Examine existing designs: check whether the design appears new and sufficiently distinguishable.
  3. Apply: submit the application and required representation of the design for the relevant article and class.
  4. Examination: the application is examined against statutory requirements.
  5. Registration: an eligible design may be entered in the register, giving the proprietor statutory rights.

Under Section 5, an application is filed in the prescribed manner and must undergo the relevant examination process. Section 6 deals with registration in respect of particular articles.

Duration of registered-design protection

Section 11 establishes the ordinary duration of registered-design protection:

  • Initial protection: 10 years from the date of registration.
  • Extension: a further 5 years on application to the Controller before the initial 10 years expire and payment of the prescribed fee.
  • Ordinary maximum: 15 years.

In the Act, the exclusive right arising from registered-design protection is also described as copyright in the registered design. It is distinct from ordinary artistic copyright under the Copyright Act, 1957.

Piracy of a registered design

Section 22 addresses piracy of a registered design.

During the subsistence of the registered-design right, specified unauthorised commercial acts may be prohibited. These include applying the registered design or a fraudulent or obvious imitation to relevant articles for sale, or importing such articles for sale without consent, subject to the Act.

For example, if a manufacturer reproduces another proprietor's protected ornamental product appearance on articles within the protected class for commercial sale, the conduct may amount to piracy under Section 22.

Industrial relevance

Industrial-design protection is relevant to manufacturing industries because product appearance influences consumer preference and product differentiation.

Possible applications include household goods, furniture, containers, textiles and other manufactured articles possessing eligible visual features.

In Gujarat, the distinction is relevant to producers of decorative household goods and modern textile products. An original visual pattern applied industrially may raise design-registration questions, while the underlying traditional technique or mechanical process is not itself an industrial design.

Prelims focus

  • The Designs Act, 2000 is the principal statute governing industrial designs.
  • Section 2(d) defines design through qualifying visual features.
  • Section 4 contains major prohibitions on registration.
  • Section 5 concerns applications for registration.
  • Section 11 provides 10 years of initial protection and a possible 5-year extension.
  • Trap: The ordinary maximum design term is 15 years, not 20 years or indefinitely renewable protection.

[Sources: Designs Act, 2000, Sections 2, 4–6, 11 and 22, Intellectual Property India; Intellectual Property India, Basics of Designs, consulted 14 November 2026; NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class 11, Chapters Crafts Heritage and Colonial Rule and Crafts.]

title: Industrial Designs: Protected Features, Registration and Legal Rights
